A pair of recent studies demonstrates that we can have a continent-wide, field-scale cropland map–as long as we’re willing to think outside the box.
You won’t see crop types or irrigation patterns in this map, but you will know the extent of cropland across a country or continent. Better maps give decision-makers a clearer, more consistent picture of the land.
The spatial extent of cropland affects how we estimate food production. To know how much to expect from a particular region, we need to know how much land is cultivated there, and where.
We also need to know where agriculture is happening to allocate water resources. Agriculture is the largest consumer of freshwater globally, and groundwater depletion is a serious issue in northern China.
We see cropland change affecting long-term resource planning. Mapping a whole country or continent at 30 meters traditionally means downloading terabytes of imagery, storing it locally, preprocessing it, and running heavy computation on dedicated hardware. When we break out of that box, however, we find we can actually do much more than that–repeatedly, consistently, and affordably.
A method that behaves predictably across very different landscapes is easier to scale than one that needs to be recalibrated for each region. That’s the central bet in a new study that produced high-accuracy, 30-meter cropland extent maps for Australia and China. Led by researchers at Boston University, the effort used imagery from Landsat-8, a random forest classifier, and Google Earth Engine (GEE).
The team found that with repeated observations over a period, and some judicious compositing and feature extraction, they could do all of the following: create a binary map that distinguished cropland from everything else, produce it separately for each country, and assess it against independent reference data. The results can be refreshed as new imagery arrives.
This study builds on previous work–notably, in 2018, by Teluguntla and colleagues, published in the ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing–which showed that open Landsat data, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing made field-scale cropland mapping across entire countries feasible without well-resourced agencies.
The two studies look different, but they’re not disparate. The 2018 study was a proof-of-concept demonstration that open Landsat data, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing could make field-scale cropland mapping across entire countries feasible without well-resourced agencies. The more recent effort showed that this approach could travel to other regions.
The difference between these two maps of Australia and China, from the two studies, is less in the data than in the details. In 2018, the effort focused on proof-of-concept, so the maps are courser. In the latest study, the team was able to look more closely.
The team used multiple observations from Landsat-8 over a period instead of a single cloud-free scene, and they composited, extracted features, classified, and assessed accuracy all in GEE. For reference samples–a constant requirement in supervised classification–they leveraged cropland or non-cropland data labeled in reference datasets.
Both studies used Landsat-8 imagery, a random forest classifier, and GEE (but the code that can point at a different region with relatively little modification). Landsat-8 revisits each location about every 16 days, allowing analysts to capture land change through the growing season. The multiple spectral bands and derived measures such as vegetation indices supplied features describing the surface.
The barrier that kept many teams from attempting this sort of work was the spectre of “pixel mixing.” When the pixels are big–250 m to 1 km resolution, as in many earlier global land cover products–a single pixel can contain a mix of crops, fallow land, trees, roads, and buildings. Determining the extent of cropland is hard when fields are small, as much of China’s are.
Pixel mixing is one reason cropland maps often disagree with one another and depend on coarse satellite pixels or on national statistics that arrive late and vary in quality. A binary cropland map won’t tell you which crops are grown, or whether the land is irrigated, or how intensively it’s farmed, but knowing where cropland is helps you estimate irrigation demand, assess pressure on river basins and aquifers, and target water management.
Cropland isn’t just defined by how it looks on a single date. It’s also defined by what it does over time. Repeat mapping reveals cropland expansion, abandonment, and conversion to urban use. And a consistent method across different regions allows comparisons that national datasets with differing definitions and standards often cannot support.
Cropland mapping is not a single-step exercise. Cropland masks feed into yield models, harvest forecasts, and early warning systems for shortfalls. So you need to know more than just the extent of cropland; crop-type and irrigation mapping will provide that information and build on the same foundation. That’s a task for the future.
The fact that supervised classification quality depends on the quality and spatial coverage of reference samples is why, importantly, reference data labeled cropland or non-cropland were used to train the model and, separately, to test it. Keeping these sets independent is essential for an honest estimate of accuracy.
And while the random forest classifier isn’t the newest machine learning technique, it’s robust, fast to train, and doesn’t demand extensive tuning. It’s also good at indicating which input variables matter most, helping researchers understand what the model uses to separate cropland from other land cover.
The fact that the same code can be pointed at a different region with relatively little modification was the central bet in this study, demonstrating that open Landsat data, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing can make continent-scale cropland mapping at field-level detail practical, repeatable, and affordable.

A Kampala-based organization working in these communities is building something extraordinary, free, safe community-run resource centers. This proposal relies on a network of partners to extend what each center can do.
What we’re proposing
This project is a network of community resource centers built inside or next to the neighborhoods they serve. Each center is meant to be a welcoming, protected space, free to use and open to the children who need them most. They’d let poor and orphaned children play, learn, eat, and get basic health care. Each center is meant to be a place where parents, guardians, local leaders and youth can come together to plan, run, and oversee each center.
How are we doing that?
We’re proposing these centers as part of a larger plan, a network of community resource centers built inside or next to the neighborhoods they serve. Each center is meant to be a welcoming, protected space, free to use and open to the children who need them most.
What will we do?
- Provide secure, supervised play spaces away from the dangers of the street.
- Offer regular, balanced, nutritious meals
- Offer age-appropriate early learning activities building literacy, numeracy, and social skills
- Provide basic health care: growth monitoring, immunization follow-up, deworming, first aid, and referrals to clinics and hospitals.
- Provide knowledge and skills to build more stable lives.
- Offer vocational and small-business skills training leading to more stable income and greater independence
- Offer nutrition training on feeding infants and children well on a tight budget using locally available foods
- Offer safe-motherhood education on prenatal care, safe delivery, postnatal recovery, family planning, and newborn care, especially for young and first-time mothers
- Health facilities and practitioners: referrals, outreach clinics, maternal health services
- Educate on family planning and safe motherhood
- Inform and economically empower mothers to make choices that strengthen whole households
- Schools and educators: support learning, ease children’s transition into formal education
What’s our goal?
Children who are safe, well fed, healthy, and stimulated in their early years are better able to learn, stay in school, and grow into productive adults. Not only do we want to help children reach their potential, we want to make lasting change. A mother’s gains in confidence, knowledge, and earning ability benefit her children directly, and informed and economically empowered mothers make choices that strengthen whole households.
Our proposal aims to break the cycle at several points at once:
- By letting small children play, learn, eat, and get basic health care we’re investing in early childhood and in mothers, two of the most effective ways to improve a community’s long-term prospects
- Informed mothers who are economically empowered make choices that strengthen whole households
- Programs that depend entirely on outside funding and staff tend to fade when support ends. Programs that communities see as their own are far more likely to last
- We insist on community ownership, with centers meant to belong to the neighborhood
- Local government and community structures align the centers with public services and child-protection systems
- Where possible, caregivers and volunteers come from the surrounding area, creating jobs and building trust
- Schools and educators support learning and ease children’s transition into formal education
- Families take part in keeping the center running, reinforcing a sense that it is their center

The border collie is one of the most well known breeds around, but what sets them apart from other herding breeds like Australian shepherds or German shepherds?
Border CollieHistory
If you look at the history of any breed, it’s easy to find out why a certain breed looks the way it does. After all, that’s all the show ring is good for—making sure that a dog conforms to a certain aesthetic. However, the border collie is different. Like any breed, it does have a relatively well-documented history, but the emphasis is not on looks. Rather, the focus is all on how it works, and that gives us insight into what makes it so special.
The origins of the border collie lie in the borderlands between England and Scotland in the 17th through 19th centuries. These areas were rough, hilly terrain where sheep were a livelihood, and drovers moved livestock long distances to markets. Sometimes flocks were moved from one country to another, so drovers needed to make sure animals did not stray. That’s where sheepdogs came in, and while we can’t say for certain that they looked like what we know as border collies today, they were highly valued for their stamina, intelligence, and an instinct to gather and control their stock.
A key component of that instinct is the eye, an intense, fixed stare that exerts pressure on livestock without making physical contact. Then there’s the gather and drive, the instinct to circle wide, collect animals, and move them in a controlled line. The stalk is a low, deliberate approach that moves sheep through presence rather than force, and finally the grab-and-kill end of the predatory sequence has been largely bred out, leaving only the first few steps of the predatory sequence found in wolves and other canids: orient, eye, stalk, chase.
Many breeds have been refined around a show-ring standard, but the border collie was shaped by a working-over-looks ethos, and that means they come in a wide range of coat types, colors, ear carriages, and sizes. Adam Telfer was a Northumberland shepherd working in the 19th century, and he’s often credited with helping consolidate the border collie type through deliberate crossbreeding, and while his contribution was really fixing working traits so they reappeared reliably in each generation, not creating a particular look, his line of dogs was prized for ability and consistency, and that makes his descendants the foundation of the modern breed, later celebrated herding dogs trace back to this lineage.
The breed’s origins may lie in the borderlands, but it’s popularity rose with the creation of sheepdog trials in the 19th century and their continued popularity today. These trials let shepherds compare dogs side by side, and rewarded dogs that could move stock calmly and efficiently under pressure. Dogs that thought independently, endured bad weather, and read animal movement earned their keep and passed on their traits, and that careful selection by working shepherds with performance as the only measure of success was the early breeding story, not aimed at show ribbons but rather at a dog that could bring the flock home.
In time, working collies became regional working collies, not a standardized breed, and early accounts of breeding are patchy, so we can hold those details loosely. However, what we do know is that they were valued for stamina, intelligence, and an instinct to gather and control their stock, and that’s what was bred for. Any dog that tired quickly, panicked easily, or needed constant direction was a liability, and the traits that make border collies brilliant in a pasture can make them difficult in a typical home.
The Eye
The eye is a fixation border collies have, and it’s an intense, fixed stare that exerts pressure on livestock. However, it’s not just for sheep, and a border collie may fixate on cars, bicycles, joggers, or children. Even worse, they may show obsessive staring, chasing, or shadow and light fixation. Put that together with herding behaviors that are modified pieces of the predatory sequence found in wolves and other canids—orient, eye, stalk, chase—and you have a dog that can run the early steps of the predatory sequence with extraordinary refinement.
Combine that with a breed’s willingness to take direction from a handler, even at a distance, and a border collie bred to think all day may not only herd family members, especially kids, but create their own jobs if none are provided. Border collies are also sensitive to noise, chaos, and inconsistent handling, so a quiet life, unpredictable schedule, or limited patience for a dog with big opinions may suit another breed better, but that doesn’t mean that a border collie can’t thrive in a home. They simply need more than a daily walk.
Herding breeds are bred to work, and behaviorist Patricia McConnell has written extensively about herding breeds, and has herded with her own border collies, and she has emphasized that they are bred to work, their drive does not switch off because they live in a house. McConnell recommends that border collies be given plenty of mental work, such as training, puzzles, structured games, dog sports like agility or flyball, or ideally, actual herding. Under-stimulated border collies may show anxiety, destructiveness, restlessness, and may show obsessive staring, chasing, or shadow and light fixation.
Border Collies in the Home
When border collies are in a home, they may nip at heels, herd family members, especially kids, but if you match the dog’s needs to the reality of a home, it’s an act of kindness for both the dog and the owner. While the breed asks a lot of its people, it’s also a brilliant working partner who will return the loyalty in spades if given a chance. If the breed’s traits can make them difficult, they can also make them extraordinary with the right owner.
Border collies are brilliant and they’re bred to think all day, so if you’re not going to provide the mental work they need, they’ll invent their own. They need an owner who is consistent, active, and willing to learn how the breed thinks, because a dog bred to think all day may invent its own jobs if none are provided.
This breed is a working partner with a brilliant mind, and without a job it will find its own. Whether the dog is a competition champion or a champion couch potato, they need more than a daily walk, and matching a dog’s needs to a household’s reality is an act of kindness for both dog and owner.

The Diocese of Richmond’s Consensus Curriculum: a Framework for the Catholic Schools of our Diocese
The Consensus Curriculum is a framework for the Catholic schools of our Diocese. While each school has room to respond to the individual needs of its own community, there are shared expectations that we aim to deliver consistently across our schools. Consistency gives families the confidence that a child moving between Catholic schools in our diocese will meet a recognizable standard. Our vision is integration, the work of faith and reason together. Truth wherever we find it will point us toward God. The Catholic worldview shapes how our students approach literature, history, science, and the arts. The Diocese of Richmond’s Consensus Curriculum is a framework for its Catholic schools.
Faith is the lens through which every subject in the Consensus Curriculum is taught. Our goal is to form young people who think clearly, live virtuously, and understand themselves as children of God called to serve others. Catholic education aims to form young people who are capable, confident, kind, prayerful, and ready to serve.
The Coherence of Catholic Education
The design of the Diocese of Richmond’s Consensus Curriculum rests on the conviction that a child is a whole person to be formed in intellect, body, heart, and soul. We place significant trust in the teachers who, in a Catholic school, are not only content experts but also witnesses to the faith. They must be skilled and faithful. Students learn from how their teacher treats a struggling classmate, handles a conflict, or responds to a hard question. Teachers serve as both witnesses to the faith and content experts who find natural, honest connections between subject matter and faith.
The role of parents and families in Catholic education is significant. The Church teaches that parents are the primary educators of their children. Principals must lead both academically and spiritually, connecting the school to the diocese, the parish, and the families. They must serve as both instructional leader and spiritual leader of the school community, communicating the curriculum’s goals to parents and inviting them into the shared work of forming their children. As spiritual leaders, principals shape a school culture where prayer, sacraments, service, and Catholic identity are lived realities.
Catholic education aims to form young people who think clearly, live virtuously, and understand themselves as children of God called to serve others. Our desire is that the family life program will be a support to parents, not a replacement for them. Families should check with their school about how it communicates with parents and how it handles questions about family life content.
The road to this desired result requires that students be challenged to grow in knowledge and in virtue. They must be pushed to learn about the natural world, the natural goodness of the human body, and what it means to be human in a world where we can easily forget that we are made in the image and likeness of God. How do we talk about this with children? In a novel a student can be led to wonder about conscience, sacrifice, and redemption. In a lesson on the natural world a student can be led to wonder at the order of creation. In a history unit a student can be led to conversation about human dignity, justice, and the common good. These are examples of how Catholic education can make the curriculum’s goals come alive.
The Consensus Curriculum
Intellectual
The intellectual goal of our Catholic schools is mastery of foundational skills in reading, writing, mathematics, and scientific reasoning, built progressively from early grades through middle school. The spiritual goal is to foster a love of learning, so that curiosity outlasts any single grade level or exam. The faith-filled curriculum places significant trust in teachers to plan carefully, use varied methods, assess progress, and adjust when students need more support or more challenge. The material is framed by Catholic teaching about the dignity of the human person and the goodness of the body as created by God. The older-year content includes more mature discussions of growth, responsibility, and the meaning of human sexuality. The younger-year content covers self-worth, friendship, and family relationships.
English/Language Arts covers reading, writing, grammar, speaking, and listening. Intellectual goal: effective written and spoken communication, expressing ideas with clarity and charity
Mathematics runs the gamut from number sense and operations to pre-algebra and beyond. Intellectual goal: mastery of foundational skills in reading, writing, mathematics, and scientific reasoning
Science covers life, earth, and physical sciences, with an emphasis on inquiry and observation. Intellectual goal: moral reasoning, applying knowledge to real decisions about how to live
Social Studies covers history, geography, civics, and economics, including Virginia and U.S. history. Intellectual goal: critical thinking, so that students can analyze arguments, weigh evidence, and reach sound conclusions
Fine Arts covers music and visual art as expressions of beauty and creativity. Intellectual goal: expanding appreciation for beauty and creativity
World Languages, where offered, reflect openness to other cultures and the universal Church. Intellectual goal: expanding appreciation for beauty and creativity
Technology and Information Literacy covers responsible, ethical, and effective use of digital tools. Intellectual goal: mastery of foundational skills in reading, writing, mathematics, and scientific reasoning
Religion is given a distinct place in the school day. Intellectual goal: moral reasoning, applying knowledge to real decisions about how to live

A suggested visit to Dunkeld starts at the font, following the street down to the cathedral and Telford’s bridge. Take less than an hour.
Dunkeld was an important ecclesiastical centre in early medieval Scotland, but after the Reformation it fell into partial ruin, the cathedral choir remaining in use as the parish church while the ruined nave stood beside it. Much of the land and property around the cathedral came under the family’s control over time and, as the authority of old church structures declined, their influence over the town grew. Through the nineteenth century the estate shaped the street layout, setting of the cathedral and the wider landscape around the town. Historically towns like Dunkeld relied on wells, springs and the river for water, carried by hand and of uncertain quality. The gift of water running to their homes from the Atholl estate was a practical improvement to daily life, a gift recognised by the townspeople as such, commemorated in stone.
The Atholl Memorial Fountain is a stone fountain standing in the middle of Dunkeld’s square. It commemorates George Murray, 6th Duke of Atholl, who died in 1864, and stands as a lasting reminder of the water supply his family brought to the town. In the evening when the light is low, the fountain’s play is visible, a sharp reminder of how much the town still relies on the generosity of the estate.
The title Duke of Atholl was created in 1703, but Dunkeld is much older than the dukedom. The Atholl seat was Blair Castle to the north of Dunkeld, and the family held land across this part of Perthshire for centuries. The Murrays held land across this part of Perthshire for centuries and, after the Reformation, the cathedral fell into partial ruin. The church structure was pulled down but the choir remained in use as the parish church, standing beside the ruined nave. Much of the land and property around the cathedral came under the family’s control over time, and as the authority of old church structures declined their influence over the town grew. The Murrays had been in a position to shape the street layout and setting of the cathedral, but also the wider landscape around the town. The Atholl estate played a leading part in rebuilding the town, and later improvements, providing work in forestry, farming and property maintenance and supporting local institutions.
The 4th Duke of Atholl was a powerful presence in the district when Telford’s bridge across the Tay was completed in 1809, replacing ferries and giving the town a lasting connection to the south. The 4th Duke is known as the Planter Duke, for the vast numbers of larches and other conifers he planted across Atholl lands. These plantations transformed the look of the hills, becoming part of the area’s identity and drawing walkers and visitors still. The woodlands around Dunkeld still bear the mark of these plantings.
In 1689, after the Battle of Killiecrankie, Jacobite Highlanders and the Cameronian regiment fought in Dunkeld, much of the town burning in the battle. Over the following decades it was rebuilt, a row of small, sturdy cottages restored in the twentieth century by the National Trust for Scotland, hinting at the modest vernacular architecture of the post-fire town. The relationships between the estate and townspeople were unequal, as so much depended on the goodwill of one family, but paternal responsibility of this kind was common among nineteenth-century Scottish landowners. The Atholl estate provided work in forestry, farming and property maintenance, and supported local institutions. Visitors come to Dunkeld for its cathedral, for river walks and the wooded hills, but also to visit the town centre with its whitewashed cottages with neat gables and its cathedral by the water. Dunkeld was an important ecclesiastical centre in early medieval Scotland. The cathedral in its present form dates largely from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries.
The 6th Duke’s great act of public service to Dunkeld was bringing piped water to the town. A reliable supply was one of the most significant improvements a Victorian community could receive, reducing drudgery and risk of disease. The people of Dunkeld chose a fountain, a structure that delivers water, rather than a statue as their memorial to the Duke, to mark their recognition of the gift of water the estate had brought them. The water running to the homes was a gift from the estate and the fountain in the square was a visible reminder of it.

A single rechargeable battery can be reused hundreds of times, replacing a pile of disposables. Batteries contain metals that take energy to mine and process, and can leach harmful materials when not disposed of properly. Disposable batteries are used in remotes, game controllers, wireless mice, kids' toys, flashlights and smoke detectors. Buying rechargeable nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) batteries plus a charger can replace them. They cost more upfront but in frequently used devices, often pay for themselves after a handful of charges. Keeping the charger where spare batteries used to be stored makes swapping in charged batteries a habit.
One dry-erase board can replace thousands of sheets of paper over its lifetime. Notepads, sticky-note packs, grocery lists, to-do lists, phone messages, reminders – household paper is used for a few hours then thrown away. A dry-erase board in a central place such as the fridge, entryway or home office can replace them all. Even better, a shared board helps a household stay organized by showing what is needed from the store and what is happening this week.
Washable mop pads can replace disposable ones. Microfiber cloths can replace most paper towels, trap dust and grime well, often with just water, and can be machine-washed many times. A pack of them costs about the same as a few rolls of paper towels and will last for years. Keep a roll around for truly messy jobs and try to cut back. A small basket under the sink will let them go in with regular laundry.

A common mistake is to assume that a distribution center, particularly one the organization runs itself, must always earn its keep.
Most organizations still have warehouses. However, the reasons those warehouses exist might have changed over time. Product packaging might have changed, suppliers might have improved their delivery options, and demand patterns might have shifted. Your distribution center might have earned its place ten years ago, but it might not today.
Treat warehouses as tools, worth keeping only if they do a job. Use a framework that focuses on function first, and apply it repeatedly, rather than as a one-time audit.
There are four classic functions that cover most legitimate reasons for a warehouse. They suggest control, predictable availability, and a single point of contact:
Break-bulk: Your warehouse receives bulk shipments and splits them into smaller orders for the customer. For example, the customer needs smaller quantities than the supplier ships, and it is cheaper to move the bulk to one point first. This operation can reduce freight costs and the number of deliveries that the customer must receive and process.
Storage: Supply and demand can operate on different rhythms. Storage lets this happen. For example, seasonal products, long production runs, and uncertain demand justify holding inventory close to the customer.
Consolidation: Your warehouse gathers goods from many suppliers and combines them into one shipment for the customer. This operation can reduce freight costs and the number of deliveries that the customer must receive and process. Consolidation can also reduce costs if the customer buys from many sources, and combining items into fewer, fuller shipments saves more than the extra handling costs.
Value-added customization: Your warehouse labels, kits, packages, or even assembles products to customer needs, often delaying final differentiation until the last responsible moment. This work can be cheaper or more flexible to do close to the customer than at the factory, and it can reduce the risk of holding the wrong variety of product.
Information provision includes accurate inventory visibility, order status, demand signals, and tracking. This is the weakest argument for a warehouse on its own, because systems can usually provide it without buildings.
Use this framework to test your distribution center:
Start with function: Ask what the facility does that would not happen otherwise. “We have always done it this way” is a warning.
Break-bulk: Ask if the customer needs smaller quantities than the supplier ships, and if it is cheaper to move the bulk to one point first. For example, do suppliers ship products to the center, the center store them, and staff pick orders and ship them to the agencies? If so, does the center add a handling step: receive, put away, pick, pack, and ship each item a second time? This operation adds cost and delay. A central facility suggests control, predictable availability, and a single point of contact. However, if the center simply receives products, stores them, and reships them, without combining goods from many distant sources in a way that cuts freight costs, it is a detour.
Storage: Ask whether there is a genuine timing mismatch between supply and demand, and if the cost of holding stock is lower than the cost of stockouts or expedited shipping. For example, does inventory turn over quickly? Is demand steady?
Consolidation: Ask whether the customer buys from many sources, and if combining items into fewer, fuller shipments saves more than the extra handling costs. For example, does the center gather goods from many suppliers, combine them, and ship them to the agencies? If so, does this operation save money on freight costs and the number of deliveries that the customer must receive and process? Alternatively, could the center fail this test because suppliers already pack office goods in the quantities that agencies buy, so nothing needs to be broken down into smaller lots?
Value-added customization: Is there work that is cheaper or more flexible to do close to the customer than at the factory? For example, does the center add a handling step: every item is received, put away, picked, packed, and shipped a second time? Or does the center perform special labeling, kit, package, assemble, or configure products to customer needs? Sometimes, delaying final differentiation can reduce the risk of holding the wrong variety of product.
The sensible answer for this case was elimination: have the suppliers ship directly to the agencies, or use a distributor that already offers consolidated delivery.
Customers receive the same products that they could have received directly from the supplier, but later and at higher cost. The center added a handling step: every item was received, put away, picked, packed, and shipped a second time. This operation added cost and delay. However, agencies received the same products they could have received directly from the supplier, but later and at higher cost.
These tests identify the function that the facility adds, if any. There might not be a function. A facility can look busy and still add no value.
Finally, consider information provision. Is the information still available, at similar quality, if the building disappeared? For example, can order tracking run through suppliers or software? Information is the weakest argument for a warehouse on its own, because systems can usually provide it without buildings. However, accurate inventory visibility, order status, demand signals, and tracking are important services, supporting one or more of the physical functions above.
These tests identify what the facility does that would not happen otherwise. It fails the test if you can answer “yes” to these questions:
- Does the facility fail every test?
- Would the facility be overhead, not a strategic asset?
There are many reasons to have a warehouse. However, those reasons can change over time. Apply this framework repeatedly, rather than as a one-time audit.

It comes from many smaller efforts: neighbourhood conversation circles, hiring policies that take overseas credentials seriously, school curricula taught partly in an Indigenous language, local councils bringing new arrivals and long-time residents together. When carried out well, it improves social cohesion efforts in host communities around refugee settlements, and reduces stigma most when people meet as equals with shared goals. Bringing people together also works well when done in the context of early education, where mother-tongue programs help Indigenous children transition into school without losing their languages, and when newcomers are paired with established professionals in their field, as in mentorship schemes in Canada. Inclusion programs for Roma communities also work best when addressing housing, schooling, and employment together, since tackling one alone rarely holds.

It's one of the simplest first steps toward preventing cardiovascular disease — a medical condition we tend to learn about when it’s already causing harm. However, checking blood pressure at home can reveal this risk factor years before it causes problems. The challenge is for the numbers to be accurate.
Blood pressure naturally rises and falls throughout the day, so patterns matter more than individual readings. A single doctor’s office reading is only a snapshot — a week of readings can provide a much more reliable baseline, more informative than any single number. Blood pressure also tends to surge in the morning, and that surge is linked to cardiovascular events.
A full bladder can raise the reading, so empty it beforehand. Sitting quietly for at least five minutes before measuring without talking, scrolling a phone, or watching something stressful can make a difference. Pain, rushing, or being upset can temporarily push numbers up, too.
Small errors can add 10 points or more to a reading. Cuff size is one of the most overlooked sources of error. A cuff that is too large can read low. A cuff that is too small gives falsely high readings.
To check the size, measure around the middle of the upper arm and compare with the size range printed on the cuff or in the manual. Most devices come with a standard cuff; larger or smaller sizes are sold separately.

- Place the cuff on bare skin, not over clothing.
- Keep the arm relaxed and supported by the table, with your palm facing upward.
- Measure twice a day — morning and evening, with two readings each time, one minute apart. Record both with the date and time. Many guidelines suggest discarding the first day’s results and averaging the rest. If you have diagnosed high blood pressure or your doctor requests monitoring, take readings for about seven days before a medical appointment or after a medication change.

As the students of East Otago High School (EOHS) prepare to embark on their language-learning journey, here’s what you can expect from our language programmes in Te Reo Māori and German.
Offering both languages gives our students a strong sense of local identity alongside a global outlook. They also learn their own manaakitanga (hospitality and care), whanaungatanga (relationships) and kaitiakitanga (guardianship) – key concepts to understand.

Landsat’s global archive can get you a 30-meter-accurate crop extent map of Australia and China.
Satellite mapping of cropland has been left largely to governments with deep pockets. Many countries lack their own data and must rely on existing maps that often conflict or on large satellite pixels that lump crops and other land covers together. Those spotty, low-resolution maps also omit information that decision-makers need—like which crops were grown and whether they were irrigated, or if farmland has been abandoned.
A 2018 study by Chandrakant Teluguntla and colleagues showed how the free Landsat archive, a reliable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing can make country-wide, field-scale cropland mapping possible without richly funded agencies. Their study, published in the ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing, delivered accurate crop extent maps at 30-meter resolution for Australia and China. The countries are very unlike in crop systems, climate, and terrain, yet the researchers wagered that one method able to map both countries well could be carried over to other places. The result was a two-class map that separates cropland from all else, made for each country on its own and checked with independent reference data. Australia’s huge, thinly populated farming areas feature big fields, rain-fed agriculture, and irrigation clustered in certain basins. China supports a very large population on relatively little farmland, much of it split into tiny, heavily managed parcels.
The researchers put out their study using Landsat-8 images, a random forest classifier, and Google Earth Engine (GEE). Their method blends observations made over a span of time, not on one cloud-free day. Clouds can restrict the usable observations in certain regions and seasons, but Landsat-8 returns to any given spot roughly every 16 days. These return passes let analysts track how land shifts over a growing season. The observations are merged into summaries that record the seasonal plant patterns, such as the typical climb and drop of cropland greenness.

What makes land cropland is its behavior over time, not only how it looks on one day. It grows numerous decision trees using random picks of data and variables, then pools their votes. Its tools were Landsat-8 images, a random forest classifier, and Google Earth Engine (GEE). The researchers write their analysis one time and run it over vast areas with no need to move the data. GEE stores the Landsat archive along with other datasets and performs the computing on Google’s cloud systems. GEE can handle compositing, feature extraction, classification, and accuracy assessment all in one place.
The team drew on many Landsat-8 observations over a span of time, not one cloud-free image. That’s necessary to expose shifts in cropland, which influences long-range planning of resources. The researchers could not examine every available Landsat-8 observation. Separating training data from test data is necessary to get a truthful accuracy figure. Labeled reference data that mark cropland or non-cropland were trained the model and were also kept apart to evaluate it. Unlike traditional land cover mapping, the researchers’ two-class map omits which crops are grown, if land is irrigated, or how intensely it is farmed. But knowing the cropland footprint helps in estimating irrigation needs, judging stress on river basins and aquifers, and directing water management. The existence of a binary cropland map is necessary to estimate the country’s food output, and that requires knowing the amount of cultivated land and where it is. This evergreen mask serves as input to yield models, harvest forecasts, and early warning systems for shortages. In Australia, for example, the country constantly faces questions about water allocation, while northern China faces a serious problem of groundwater depletion.
Farming uses more freshwater than any other sector worldwide, so knowing the cropland footprint aids in estimating irrigation needs, judging stress on river basins and aquifers, and directing water management.
Numerous earlier worldwide land cover datasets relied on images with 250 meters to 1 kilometer resolution. That’s sharp enough to blend crops, idle land, trees, roads, and buildings into one pixel. The result was maps that frequently conflict, rely on large satellite pixels, or lean on national figures that come late and differ in quality.
At 30 meters, Landsat-8 gives pixels sharp enough to separate single fields in many farming zones. Mapping an entire country or continent at 30 meters used to require downloading terabytes of images, keeping them on local storage, preprocessing them, and running intensive computing on specialized machines.

The Diocese of Richmond’s Consensus Curriculum: a Structure Guiding Its Catholic Schools
The Diocese of Richmond’s Consensus Curriculum offers a broad framework for our Catholic schools to serve as a structure guiding them. These schools are all different, but all share certain expectations. It serves to help principals lead the school community both in teaching and learning, as well as in spiritual life.
The Curriculum offers a range of subjects typical of an elementary/middle school program. Teachers are expected to bear witness to the faith as well as to know their subjects. This curriculum is built on the belief that each child is a whole person who must be formed in mind, body, heart and soul.
This material rests on the Catholic teaching about the dignity of the human person and the goodness of the body as God made it. English/Language Arts includes reading, writing, grammar, speaking, and listening. The goal of this curriculum is to develop strong writing and speaking abilities, so that students can convey their ideas clearly and with charity.
Mathematics progresses from number sense and operations through pre-algebra and further. In Social Studies we include history, geography, civics, and economics among other things Virginia and U.S. history. These subjects can spark discussions on the worth of every person, fairness, the common good, and more.
In Science we have the life, earth and physical sciences, stressing inquiry and observation. Studying nature can bring students to marvel at how creation is ordered. In Religion we have Scripture, doctrine, sacraments, prayer, morality, and Catholic social teaching. These discussions can also raise questions of conscience, self-giving, and redemption when studied through a novel. Fine Arts includes music and visual art as ways of expressing beauty and creativity. Technology and Information Literacy help students learn to use digital tools responsibly, ethically, and well. Physical Education and Health show concern for the body as part of caring for the entire person.
The curriculum puts great trust in its teachers, who are expected to prepare thoughtfully, vary their approaches, measure progress, and change course when students require extra help or greater challenge. They also draw genuine, truthful links between what they teach and the faith.
The role of the principal is to be a leader in both academic and spiritual matters. Principals are stewards of a school’s culture, where prayer, sacraments, service, and Catholic identity are part of daily life. They also need to guide in both academic and spiritual matters. In their academic role, principals make sure the curriculum is put into practice, visit classrooms, back teachers’ professional development, examine student progress, and confirm that standards become real learning. In their spiritual role, principals build a school culture where prayer, sacraments, service, and Catholic identity are part of daily life.
In a Catholic school, what the teacher models is part of what is taught. Students learn by watching how the teacher handles a classmate in difficulty, deals with disagreement, or answers a tough question. The faith colors the way students engage with literature, history, science, and the arts.
In their spiritual role, principals share the curriculum’s aims with parents and welcome them to join in the common effort of forming their children. In their academic role, principals need to help teachers link their lessons to the diocesan standards, turning diocesan standards into everyday lessons suited to their students.
The goal is unity: faith and reason cooperate, and any truth, wherever it turns up, leads to God. The curriculum sees academic excellence as one piece of living faithfully.
The series introduced here seeks to introduce topics suited to each age across the grades. The content for older years covers more mature talks about growth, responsibility, and what human sexuality means. For younger years, the focus is on self-worth, friendship, and family relationships. The hope is that this leads to young people who are able, self-assured, kind, prayerful, and prepared to serve.

Dunkeld became a tourist destination
Dunkeld sits at a pleasant spot along the banks of the River Tay. There’s a small town here in Perthshire, made up of white-painted cottages with tidy gables, plus a cathedral that stands beside the water. Across the city centre’s square there is a fountain made out of stone. It’s a common thing for people visiting Dunkeld to start their tours at the fountain – and how could they do so, for it is Dunkeld’s central spot for meeting, resting, and taking pictures. In a small town, choices made by the family in charge could determine the shape of housing, the village school and everything else. In Dunkeld, that job belonged to the Atholl family.
The Atholl Memorial Fountain
The Atholl Memorial Fountain in Dunkeld was built in 1866 to honor George Murray, the 6th Duke of Atholl, who passed away in that year. Instead of raising a statue to him, the town residents chose to remember him with a fountain that supplies water. Historically, towns such as Dunkeld got their water from wells, springs, and the river, but these were hauled by hand, and how clean they were could not be trusted. With the Atholl family’s water supply, it was a whole new and more practical boost to everyday life, and the town chose to commemorate it in stone.

Dunkeld, which came long before the dukedom
Throughout this area of Perthshire, the Murrays owned land for hundreds of years. As the power of the church bodies in the early medieval period gave way to them, the Atholl family eventually came to control most of the land and buildings near the cathedral. In Dunkeld, this meant that the town’s residents were not equals, for so much rested on a single family’s goodwill.
As all of Scotland was in upheaval, Dunkeld also fell into this mix. In the year 1689, Jacobite Highlanders and the Cameronian regiment clashed in the town, and fire destroyed most of it. Following this, the ruined nave partly stood alongside, but the cathedral’s choir continued serving as the parish church. Over the next several decades, the town was built anew. The present Dunkeld cathedral mostly comes from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries. Yet the estate’s care of the cathedral grounds helped to ensure that the site would survive. Today, Dunkeld continues to draw people for its cathedral, riverside walks, and wooded hills, which still show the effect of the plantings put in by the 4th Duke of Atholl.

Across Atholl lands, the 4th Duke put in huge quantities of larches and other conifers. These plantations changed how the hills look and became part of the area’s identity. To this day, these woods still show the effect of these plantings. For a Victorian community, dependable piped water ranked among the biggest of gains, as it cut down on toil and the danger of illness. He went down as the “Planter Duke”.

The American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology 2018 high blood pressure guideline pushes back the cutoffs for hypertension (high blood pressure) from 140/90 mm Hg to 130/80 mm Hg. The challenge is that the numbers never rise to that degree, and elevated pressure in the blood seldom brings pain, light-headedness, or any clear sign.
But elevated pressure can make a heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, or heart failure more likely, so this article offers general information and does not replace professional medical advice. Across many years, elevated pressure overworks the heart and harms the arterial walls.
Why Test at Home
Testing at home reveals how pressure acts over normal days, free of the tension of a clinic visit. Checking at home only takes minutes, but it can expose a risk factor years before damage occurs.
Who Should Test at Home?
Doctors and nurses can guide what to do on the monitoring plan and goals that fit each person. But if you have a high blood pressure diagnosis or your doctor asked for monitoring, record readings for roughly seven days ahead of a medical appointment or following a change in medication. And if you have no diagnosis but are past age 40 or have risks like family history, diabetes, excess weight, or kidney disease, you may gain from occasional checks at home.
1) Use one arm every time, ideally the one with higher readings. If the doctor directs otherwise, stick with what they say.
2) Sit on a chair that has a back, keeping your back upright and resting against it. Set both feet flat on the ground, legs not crossed. Checking at home can disclose how pressure acts over normal days, free of the tension of a clinic visit.
3) Get a validated monitor and think about taking it to an appointment to check it against the clinic's equipment. Some monitors ship with a standard cuff; bigger or smaller ones are purchased separately. If you don't know the size, measure around the midpoint of the upper arm and compare it with the range printed on the cuff or in the manual. Cuff size is among the most commonly missed causes of error, with an oversized cuff producing low readings and an undersized one yielding falsely high numbers.
4) Put the cuff on uncovered skin, not on top of clothes. The lower edge goes about an inch over the elbow crease, and the tube runs down the inner arm. A sleeve pushed up tight should not squeeze like a tourniquet.
5) Set the arm on a table or desk, keeping the center of the cuff level with the heart. An arm dropped lower than the heart yields a falsely high number, while one lifted higher than the heart results in a falsely low one.
6) Remain motionless and silent as the device fills with air. Discomfort, hurrying, or feeling upset can briefly lift the numbers.
7) Take a pair of readings one minute apart and write down both along with date and time. Make the two times identical every day so results can be compared. Don't test nonstop; that can feed worry and cause overreaction to ordinary ups and downs.
8) Empty your bladder first; a full bladder can push the number up.
9) Allow at least 30 minutes after caffeine, smoking, exercise, or alcohol prior to testing.

For adults acting ahead of problems, a week of readings every several months, or any time a clinic number runs high, is sensible.
What to Bring to a Medical Appointment
If you have your own monitor, take it to an appointment to check it against the clinic's equipment. If you don't, ask the doctor or nurse to help you pick a validated monitor and reserve a week to give the results to a healthcare provider.
If you have seven days of data, never diagnose yourself or change medication alone; bring the log to the appointment, so the clinician sees the whole pattern.

The paper title is A 30-m landsat-derived cropland extent product of Australia and China using random forest machine learning algorithm on Google Earth Engine cloud computing platform. The study developed a Landsat 30-m derived cropland extent product for Australia and China.
The study used eight bands of Landsat-8 16-day Operational Land Imager (OLI) data: blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2, TIR1, and NDVI. Each band was time-composited over 4–6 time-periods per year using median value for various agro-ecological zones (AEZs) of Australia and China.
The classification used a pixel-based supervised random forest (RF) machine learning algorithm (MLA) executed on the Google Earth Engine (GEE) cloud computing platform. The croplands versus non-croplands knowledge base for training the RF algorithm was derived from the MFDC.
Compositing produced a 32–48-layer mega-file data-cube (MFDC) for each AEZ. The cropland class was derived by applying the RF algorithm on the MFDC. The cropland class was verified using independent validation samples: 900 for Australia and 1972 for China.
The study resulted in a paradigm-shift in how cropland maps are produced using multi-date remote sensing. The study improved upon the methodology which resulted in the above mentioned paper. The performance of the study was assessed using independent validation samples: 900 for Australia and 1972 for China. The study resulted in the cropland extent products capturing the individual farm fields, small or large. The study resulted in very important, distinct, diverse and large countries, Australia and China.
The study resulted in cropland extent products with accuracy exceeding 94%. The accuracy was assessed with independent validation samples: 900 for Australia and 1972 for China. The border collie is considered the most iconic breed of working stock dog. They’re often referred to as the quintessential sheepdog, but they can work any type of stock, including sheep, cattle, poultry, and pigs. The breed’s ability to work stock makes them the stock dog of choice for ranchers across the globe.
Working border collie registries include dogs of all shapes, sizes, and coat types. It’s not uncommon to see single-minded dogs of the working stock type who are incredibly focused on their work, despite the presence of distractions, but this single-mindedness can also make these dogs prone to obsessive behaviors.
Border collie history
The ancestry of border collies traces back to rough drover dogs used in the border country between England and Scotland from the 17th to the 19th century. In the late 19th century, shepherd Adam Telfer decided to experiment with crossing the coarse drover dogs with the milder-mannered working collie. The cross resulted in a dog named Old Hemp, who was powerful yet biddable. Old Hemp became the progenitor of the border collie breed.
Border collies are bred to listen to their handlers from far away while in a hyperfocused state, so they are very sound- and motionsensitive. They may not be the best match for families with children or for busy, boisterous households.
Border collie traits
Border collies working stock have to have the perfect mixture of balance—the ability to find the exact right point in space and put the exact right amount of pressure on the sheep—and power. They have to be benevolent leaders that can take charge without panicking the sheep. Border collies are bred to listen to their handlers from far away while in a hyperfocused state, so they are very sound- and motionsensitive. They may not be the best match for families with children or for busy, boisterous households.
If you give them a job, such as working stock, racing through an agility course, or leaping after a highflying Frisbee, border collies can be great dogs both on and off the farm.
Border collie suitability
Border collies are not a dog for everyone. They need a lot of exercise—mental, too, not just physical. Although they are not the ideal choice for homes with children or busy households, they can be great in the right environment. Border collies given a job such as working stock, racing through an agility course, or leaping after a highflying Frisbee can be great dogs both on and off the farm.

The Atholl Memorial Fountain is situated in the old part of Dunkeld in the Cathedral Precinct. Built in 1866 ‘to the memory of George Augustus Frederick John 6th Duke of Atholl’ it was funded by public subscription and is the work of C S Robertson. The Fountain was erected on the site of the Market Cross (which is now the site of the War Memorial). The former site of the Market Cross was swept away when much of Dunkeld was re-built after the Battle of Dunkeld (1689).
The carvings in the Fountain have fine detail and include native animals and birds. Masonic symbols are incorporated in the Fountain and prior to being erected on the site of the Market Cross was situated near the Wynds which lead to the water because all the water for Dunkeld was drawn from the River Tay. It was designed to commemorate the 6th Duke, who introduced a piped water supply to Dunkeld, and also to commemorate his wife, Duchess Anne, who founded a girls’ school in 1854. Katharine used her Parliamentary salary to renovate some of the houses in Dunkeld. The girls’ school building still bears her name.
The 6th Duke was Grand Master Mason of Scotland from 1843 until his death in 1864 and it is thought that a masonic lodge was situated on the site of the Fountain. Ownership of the Fountain was publicly transferred to the National Trust for Scotland in 1991 in a ceremony conducted by the 10th Duke of Atholl and attended by his Atholl Highlanders. The 8th Duke was the first President of the National Trust for Scotland. The 10th Duke of Atholl had a long association with the Trust and was President at the time of his death in 1996.
The Little Houses in the Cross and Cathedral Street were given to the National Trust for Scotland by Atholl Estates in 1954. They were near-derelict, but the Trust and the Local Authority restored them to provide homes for local people. The Fountain was also restored by the Trust and its water supply re-created the 17th-century approach to the setting of the Cathedral of St. Columba. Generous assistance for the restoration came from the Duke of Atholl, the Atholl Highlanders, various charitable trusts and individuals, the Perth & Kinross Members’ Group (NTS) and Dunkeld & Birnam Community Council.
The Atholl Family have had a long and significant connection with the Dunkeld area and its people. Successive Dukes gradually acquired many Dunkeld properties during the 18th and 19th centuries. Stanley Hill was landscaped by the 2nd Duke in 1730. Duchess Anne, widow of the 6th Duke, founded a girls’ school in 1854.
The 8th Duke was the first President of the National Trust for Scotland. His wife, Katharine, was Scotland’s first woman MP. The 10th Duke was President of the Trust at the time of his death in 1996.

A study found that it would be cheaper and quicker to order office supplies directly from the wholesaler instead of the organization’s distribution center. The organization immediately decided to terminate the distribution center.
Without distribution centers an immense production capacity would be required to meet peak demand. Prices and supply of seasonal products would fluctuate wildly.
There’s a subset of the goods flow for which the distribution center doesn’t add value. So, what happens if the distribution center is eliminated? Would customer service be negatively impacted? Would overall supply chain costs increase? The organization’s distribution center did not support any of the four basic warehouse functions and therefore it only added costs, not value.
A non-profit organization held a central inventory of office supplies. The organization studied what would happen if the branches ordered their office supplies directly from the wholesaler. It was found that it would be cheaper and quicker if the branches ordered directly from the wholesaler. So, the organization immediately decided to terminate its distribution center.
The purpose of this study was to find out whether the distribution center added value or not. The distribution center failed to support any of the four basic warehouse functions, so it only added costs, not value. In such a case, the organization should consider eliminating the distribution center.
In most instances a distribution center adds value to the supply chain. To justify the need for a distribution center it should first be evaluated with respect to the four basic warehouse functions. They are:
- Break-bulk: enables products to arrive in large quantities and be shipped in small quantities
- Storage: helps manage time delays between supply and demand
- Consolidation: improves customer service since goods are received in a single delivery
- Value added services: provide better service to customers
Break-bulk creates economies of scale in production, purchasing, and inbound transportation. Break-bulk improves customer service since customers can order the specific quantity they want. Consolidation increases the efficiency of outbound transportation. It allows customers to order a large product range from a single source. Storage for demand anticipation makes products available during peak demand, e.g., toys in December. Storage for instant availability furnishes customer demand within short response times and improves customer service.
The consolidation function means that the distribution center holds products from various sources. Postponing customization services until the end of the supply chain reduces inventories upstream. Speculation inventory, often raw materials, is held because prices are expected to rise. Strategic products inventory covers essential products with uncertain supply, e.g., rare metals.
A prominent aspect of each of the four basic warehouse functions is information provision. Information provision gives value to the supply chain.
Value Added Services
A distribution center adds value through physical activities but also by gathering and maintaining related information and informing supply chain partners as required.
Let’s consider the following case study of a distribution center with a break-bulk function for only 50 percent of its volume.
The distribution center has been used as a buffer for an organization’s branches. The branches can order from the distribution center. This function was found by a study to be redundant. It was cheaper and quicker if the branches ordered directly from the wholesaler. However, the distribution center provided other useful functions.
The distribution center enabled economies of scale in production, purchasing, and inbound transportation.
The consolidation function provided customer service. The customers could order a large product range from a single source. Consolidation also improved the efficiency of outbound transportation.
Consolidation provides customer service since goods are received in a single delivery.
There may be a subset of the goods flow for which the distribution center does not add value. However, for the remaining 50 percent of its volume, the distribution center provided other functions.
The distribution center provides economies of scale in production, purchasing, and inbound transportation.
The distribution center holds products from various sources.
The break-bulk function provides better customer service since customers can order the specific quantity they want.
Storage for demand anticipation makes products available during peak demand.
The organization’s distribution center only incurred costs and increased response times. However, it failed to support any of the four functions. Therefore, it only added costs, not value. So, the organization immediately decided to terminate its distribution center.
This leads to the following conclusion. There may be a subset of the goods flow for which the distribution center does not add value. So, what happens if the distribution center were eliminated? Would customer service be negatively impacted? Would overall supply chain costs increase? Whether a distribution center is needed should first be justified by evaluating the four basic warehouse functions. Distribution centers add value through physical activities but also by gathering and maintaining related information and informing supply chain partners as required. However, in such cases where the distribution center fails to support one or several of the warehouse functions, the supply chain manager should consider eliminating the distribution center.

Q: How do I measure my blood pressure, and how often do I need to?
A: Almost 1 out of every 3 Americans has high blood pressure, also known as hypertension. That equates to over 100 million Americans with this condition. While many may not realize the impact hypertension has on our health, it can cause serious health problems, such as heart attack and stroke – and is the leading cause of death worldwide. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in the United States.
Fortunately, measuring your blood pressure and taking steps to lower it if necessary can help prevent cardiovascular disease.
Monitoring your blood pressure regularly is important. Even if you don’t have hypertension, it’s smart to check your blood pressure at least once every year during your annual physical. At minimum, your blood pressure should be checked once every year at a doctor visit.
If you have hypertension, it’s a good idea to check your blood pressure more often – and to monitor it twice a day until your blood pressure is under control. Once your blood pressure is under control, you should keep testing it to monitor your heart health, but you can reduce the frequency of your monitoring. It’s important to keep in mind that your monitoring schedule should fit your health condition and monitoring needs.
Before you get started, make sure you follow the instructions that come with your monitor. Follow these simple steps to measure your blood pressure.
1. Sit with your back straight and supported. Place your feet flat on the floor and keep your legs uncrossed.
2. Rest your testing arm on a flat supportive surface, with the upper arm at chest level.
3. Slide the cuff onto your arm, making sure the bottom of the cuff is under your clothing and just above the elbow. Make sure the size of the cuff is two-thirds of the length of your arm from your elbow to your shoulder.
4. Before testing your blood pressure, avoid exercise, smoking and caffeinated beverages for at least thirty minutes. You should also use the restroom before your test.
5. Take two to three readings each time you test your blood pressure.
6. Test your blood pressure at the same time every day, whether it’s in the morning or evening. If you test it at the end of the day, your blood pressure will likely be higher, because you’ve been moving around more and have dealt with the stress of the day.
It’s important to use a quality machine to get accurate readings. Using the wrong size cuff, or an arm that’s above your heart, can give you a falsely low reading.
Make sure to take your blood pressure when your arm is at heart level, to eliminate gravity’s influence on the reading. It’s also important to use the right arm each time you take your blood pressure.
If you have hypertension, consult with your doctor to determine how often you should measure your blood pressure. With your health history in mind, your doctor will be able to recommend a frequency that fits your needs. With the right plan, you’ll be on your way to keeping your heart healthy.

At East Otago High School we offer a range of programmes, including Te Reo and German programmes. This blog entry focuses on the Te Reo and German programmes offered at EOHS.
Te Reo
Te Reo is offered from year 7 to 10. Year 10 students can choose to study German. In Year 10 students have 2 periods a week for the full year. The Year 10 Te Reo programme prepares students with confidence and skill to study NCEA Level 1 by correspondence. Students will have the tools to develop the confidence and skills needed to study Te Reo at NCEA Level 1. The students use text books Te Reo Take Take and Te Matapuna more formally.
The Year 7 and 8 Te Reo programme is based on an odd/even year cycle. In the even year (focus on Kai/ food) students have a Te Reo lesson once a week for two terms. In the odd year (focus on Te Marae/ the marae) students have two periods for two terms. In Year 9 Te Reo is an option. In Year 9 one group focuses on Matariki and the second group studies Parihaka. Year 9 students have two periods of Te Reo for two terms. They study the structure of sentences and simple conversations. They build on the basics covered in the junior school.
German
East Otago High School offers a German programme for Year 7 and 8. The Year 7 and 8 German programme is a two year programme. The key aim of the programme is to introduce students to another language and culture. In the first year students have German lessons twice a week for a third of the year. The year begins with an introduction to basic vocabulary and key phrases. They learn to introduce themselves and talk about their family, age, birthday, where they are from, and their house. They learn to count to 100 and say the German alphabet. They are introduced to German life and culture through the Ministry of Education’s ‘Ja’ series. Alongside this students build a basic Kupu Hou (word bank) covering greetings and simple questions about families, friends and classroom. In the second year students continue to learn about differences and similarities between New Zealand and German culture. They learn to talk about school subjects, pets, hobbies, sport, and food. They also learn how to tell the time.
In Year 9 German is an option. This programme builds on the knowledge and ability developed in Year 7 and 8. Year 9 German focuses on the skills Listening, Reading, Speaking and Writing. They continue to learn about similarities and differences between German and New Zealand culture. They extend their vocabulary and cover a diverse range of topics often based around the ‘Katzensprung’ textbooks and workbooks. There is always close liaison with the local marae. German speaking countries such as Germany, Switzerland, Austria, and Liechtenstein are mentioned. In Year 10 students can choose to study German. In Year 10 students have 3 German lessons a week for 2 terms. In this year students develop the foundation they need in order to study German as an NCEA subject.

A 30-m landsat-derived cropland extent product of Australia and China using random forest machine learning algorithm on Google Earth Engine cloud computing platform
This paper's authors bring news about mapping cropland extent at continental scale with 30-meter Landsat imagery on Google Earth Engine.
Gumma Murali Krishna heads the GIS and Remote Sensing Lab at ICRISAT. Gumma is among the authors of a paper about mapping at continental scale with 30-meter Landsat imagery on Google Earth Engine.
Teluguntla Pardhasaradhi, Thenkabail Prasad, Oliphant Anna, Xiong Jian, Gumma Murali Krishna, Congalton Robert G., Huete Ariel, Shahidullah Ahmed, Kshirsagar Rani, Zhang Bing, Song Qi, and Zhang Xiu-Juan. “A 30-m landsat-derived cropland extent product of Australia and China using random forest machine learning algorithm on Google Earth Engine cloud computing platform.” ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing, 144, 325-340, 2018. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isprsjprs.2018.07.017
The paper characterizes its study as a paradigm-shift in the way multi-date remote sensing is used to produce cropland maps. The independent validation samples of 900 for Australia and 1972 for China were used to check accuracy. The total accuracy was above 94%. For Australia, the cropland class showed producer’s accuracy of 98.8% (errors of omissions = 1.2%) and user’s accuracy of 79% (errors of commissions = 21%). For China, the cropland class showed producer’s accuracy of 80% (errors of omissions = 20%) and user’s accuracy of 84.2% (errors of commissions = 15.8%). Compared to conventionally derived national statistics, the estimates ran 8.6% higher for Australia and 3.9% higher for China. The matching against China’s cropland areas by province resulted in an R2 value of 0.85, indicating the product accurately estimates cropland areas below national level.
The data, which spanned 2013–2015, were derived from eight bands of Landsat-8 16-day Operational Land Imager (OLI) data: blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2, TIR1, and NDVI. For each band, median values were used to composite over time into 4–6 periods per year, for the various agro-ecological zones (AEZs) of Australia and China. This compositing yielded a mega-file data-cube (MFDC) of 32–48 layers for every AEZ. The MFDC supplied the knowledge base separating croplands from non-croplands to train the RF algorithm. Training relied on 958 reference-training samples for Australia and 2130 for China. Reference data for training and validation came from visits to fields, very high spatial resolution imagery (VHRI) from sub-meter to 5-m, and supporting sources like National agriculture bureaus.
Difficulties in mapping cropland over big areas include enormous data volumes, computing power, and gathering reference training and validation data, which takes lots of resources, across complicated geographic and political boundaries. The above-mentioned paper uses a supervised, pixel-based random forest (RF) machine learning algorithm (MLA) run on the Google Earth Engine (GEE) cloud computing platform. The cropland products pick up each separate farm field, whether tiny or huge. Anyone can get the data products at no cost from USGS website at https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/node/1282. Downloads of the products are offered by NASA's Land Processes Distributed Active Archive Center (LP DAAC) https://www.lpdaac.usgs.gov/node/1282.

The classic sheep-herding dog, the border collie stands as the top emblem among working stock dog breeds. Ranchers worldwide pick the working border collie as their top stock dog.
Border collie roots go back to tough drover’s dogs that worked the border country between England and Scotland from the 17th to the 19th century. The drover dogs were hard to control and rough on the animals.
In the late 19th century, shepherd Adam Telfer tried mating the rugged drover dogs with the gentler working collie, and the pairing yielded a dog called Old Hemp.
The dog was strong but willing to obey, and he became the founding sire of the border collie breed. Ranchers worldwide pick the working border collie as their top stock dog.
Border Collie’s History is Like a Genetics 101 Experiment
The history of the border collie breed is like a genetics 101 experiment: one devoted to breeding for ability to work instead of adherence to a physical “breed standard.”
The registries of working border collies list dogs in every shape, size, and coat type. “The ideal working border collie has the perfect mixture of balance—the ability to find the exact right point in space and put the exact right amount of pressure on the sheep—and power,” says Patricia McConnell, a certified applied animal behaviorist who owns working border collies.
“The history of the breed is fascinating because there are no breed standards to adhere to, so we’re only breeding for ability to work,” McConnell says. “They may not be the best match for families with children or for busy, boisterous households. They need a lot of exercise—mental, too, not just physical.”
But a border collie with a task, like herding stock, tearing through an agility course, or jumping for a highflying Frisbee, can be a fine dog on the farm and away from it. “They’re bred to listen to their handlers from far away while in a hyperfocused state, so they are very sound- and motionsensitive,” McConnell says. “It’s why they are an absolute joy to work. The one-track focus that holds border collies steady through distractions can also make them likely to develop obsessive habits.

No matter what your lifestyle, a border collie’s mission will be clear. “The bottom line is that they’re bred to work, and to work hard,” McConnell says. “So pick one with a task.”
